planting.note: Set out container plants after all frost danger has passed and nights stay warm, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Sundaville Red is a compact, self-branching selection bred for hanging baskets and patio pots rather than the vigorous climbing habit of Sun Parasol types.

directions: Sundaville Red is a Japanese-bred mandevilla selected for a mounding, lightly trailing habit that fills a hanging basket or large pot without the long twining stems of standard mandevilla vines. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and water deeply whenever the top inch dries out, feeding regularly through the growing season to sustain the non-stop show of glossy, deep red, funnel-shaped flowers from late spring through fall. In zone 9 treat as a warm-season annual or bring containers indoors to a bright window before the first frost, since the plant has little cold tolerance. The milky sap can irritate skin, so wear gloves when pruning or deadheading.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension — Mandevilla
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Mandevilla Vines for the Garden
Fleuroselect — Awarded Varieties: Sundaville Series

common_name: Sundaville Cream Pink Mandevilla (Double-Shaded Trailing Dipladenia)

planting.note: Set out container plants after all frost danger has passed and nights stay warm, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; this compact Sundaville selection is bred for mounding baskets and mixed containers rather than trellising.

directions: Sundaville Cream Pink bears soft, two-toned pink blooms that fade toward a paler, creamy pink center, giving each flower a subtle shaded effect distinct from the solid-colored Rio and Sun Parasol lines. Grow it in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, keeping the root zone evenly moist and fertilizing every few weeks to keep the mounding, lightly trailing plant in continuous bloom from spring through fall. It performs best in large containers and hanging baskets where its gently cascading stems can be appreciated at eye level. Where winter temperatures approach freezing, treat as an annual or overwinter indoors in a bright, warm location.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension — Mandevilla
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Mandevilla Vines for the Garden
Fleuroselect — Awarded Varieties: Sundaville Series

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings after all frost danger has passed in fertile, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; the cream-white leaf margins are most pronounced on new growth flushed during warm, bright weather.

directions: WARNING: ALL PARTS OF THIS PLANT ARE HIGHLY TOXIC IF INGESTED — site away from children and pets and never burn the trimmings. Variegated angel's trumpet carries the same large, pendant, intensely fragrant white-to-cream trumpets as the species but with broad, irregular cream-white margins on its large leaves, adding ornamental interest even between bloom flushes. Grow it in fertile, consistently moist, well-drained soil with some afternoon shade in the hottest part of the Gulf Coast summer to prevent leaf scorch on the variegated tissue, and feed heavily through the growing season to sustain both foliage color and flowering. Where winters dip below freezing it dies back hard but usually resprouts from the base if heavily mulched; container culture allows it to be moved to shelter in cold snaps.
sources: International Brugmansia and Datura Society
San Marcos Growers
Plantlust — Brugmansia suaveolens 'Variegata'

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens after the last frost in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; this true dwarf, imported originally from the Philippines, stays densely branched with unusually short internodes rather than vining.

directions: Pink Pixie is a true dwarf bougainvillea valued for its naturally tight, bushy habit and short distance between leaf nodes, which makes it well suited to containers, borders, and bonsai-style training rather than trellising. Plant in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, since bougainvilleas bloom most heavily under mild water and fertilizer stress; overly rich soil or excess water promotes foliage at the expense of the neon-pink bracts. It tolerates heat, drought, and salt spray once established and blooms from spring through fall in zone 9, nearly year-round in truly frost-free locations. Protect from frost, which will defoliate or kill the plant outright.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Finder
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Bougainvillea

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines after the last frost against a trellis, arbor, or fence in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean soil in full sun; this vigorous glabra x peruviana hybrid needs sturdy support and regular tying-in while young.

directions: Lady Mary Baring is a vigorous climbing bougainvillea hybrid prized for its golden-yellow bracts surrounding small cream-white true flowers, a color uncommon among the more typical pinks, reds, and purples of the genus. Give it a sturdy arbor, pergola, or fence to scramble over, since in the ground it can reach well over twenty feet, though container culture keeps it to a manageable size on a trellis. Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun and withhold excess water and fertilizer once established, since bougainvilleas flower most heavily under mild stress. Protect from frost, which defoliates the vine and can kill stems to the ground.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society Plant Finder
Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Finder

common_name: Mathilde Ferrier Oleander (Hardy Double Yellow Oleander)

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in spring or set out container plants once the soil has warmed, in ordinary well-drained soil in full sun; this is among the most cold-tolerant named oleanders, grown successfully well north of typical oleander range.

directions: WARNING: ALL PARTS OF THIS PLANT ARE HIGHLY TOXIC IF INGESTED — keep it away from grazing animals and small children, and never burn the trimmings. Mathilde Ferrier is an old, large-growing oleander cultivar bearing fully double, soft primrose-yellow flowers with a sweet fragrance, a departure from the typical pink, red, or white single blooms of most oleanders. It is also sold under the older synonym 'Luteum Plenum' and has a reputation as one of the hardiest named oleanders available, tolerating brief freezes with little dieback once established. Plant in full sun in ordinary well-drained soil and allow it room to grow into a large, dense, multi-stemmed shrub, since it responds poorly to heavy repeated shearing.
sources: Plantlust — Nerium oleander 'Mathilde Ferrier'
San Marcos Growers
Almost Eden Plants

common_name: Mrs. Lucille Hutchings Oleander (Double Peach-Salmon Oleander)

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in spring or set out container plants once the soil has warmed, in ordinary well-drained soil in full sun; a vigorous, large-growing heirloom Galveston-area selection that needs ample room to reach full size.

directions: WARNING: ALL PARTS OF THIS PLANT ARE HIGHLY TOXIC IF INGESTED — keep it away from grazing animals and small children, and never burn the trimmings. Mrs. Lucille Hutchings is a long-grown Gulf Coast heirloom oleander bearing large, fully double flowers in a soft peach-to-salmon shade edged with a deeper pink, carried in generous clusters over a long summer bloom season. It is one of the larger-growing named oleanders, capable of reaching small-tree proportions along the Texas and Louisiana coast if left unpruned, so site it where it has room to mature or commit to annual thinning. Plant in full sun in ordinary, well-drained soil; once established it tolerates heat, drought, and salt spray with ease.
sources: Oleander Haus — American Oleander Cultivars
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Oleander

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in spring or set out container plants once the soil has warmed, in ordinary well-drained soil in full sun; an Algerian-origin selection introduced to the US nursery trade in the late 1970s.

directions: WARNING: ALL PARTS OF THIS PLANT ARE HIGHLY TOXIC IF INGESTED — keep it away from grazing animals and small children, and never burn the trimmings. Tangier is a medium-sized oleander of North African origin, bearing single, widely separated, medium-pink petals that give the flower a looser, more open look than many double-flowered cultivars. Its intermediate size, generally staying under six feet, makes it easier to maintain as a screening hedge or specimen shrub than large heirloom types. Plant in full sun in ordinary well-drained soil; it shares the species' tolerance of heat, drought, and salt spray once established.
sources: Oleander Haus — American Oleander Cultivars
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Oleander

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens or rooted cuttings in spring once nights stay above 60°F, in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; give this scrambling, semi-woody vine a trellis, fence, or arbor to climb, or let it sprawl as a dense groundcover.

directions: Williamsii allamanda is an older, lightly fragrant selection distinguished from the common golden trumpet vine by its semi-double to double flowers and a softer, slightly paler yellow than the typical glossy gold of the species. It is a scrambling, semi-woody vine that needs a trellis, fence, or arbor to climb, or can be left to sprawl where its weight is supported. Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and feed regularly through the growing season for continuous bloom from late spring through fall. The milky sap is toxic and can irritate skin, so wear gloves when pruning.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension — Allamanda cathartica
Plants for a Future (pfaf.org)

common_name: Yellow Firecracker Fern (Golden Coral Fountain Plant)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring once soil has warmed, in well-drained soil in full sun; this yellow-flowered selection shares the species' wiry, rush-like, nearly leafless stems and cascading habit.

directions: This yellow-flowered form of coral fountain plant produces the same fine, wiry, cascading stems as the common red-flowered species but with clusters of small, tubular, soft yellow blooms instead of coral-red, giving a lighter color option for the same drought-tough, hummingbird-friendly groundcover or trailing container plant. Grow it in full sun in well-drained soil; it tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil once established but will not tolerate wet feet in winter. Where winters dip below freezing the top growth dies back but the plant typically resprouts from the base if mulched, especially in zone 9b and warmer.
sources: Almost Eden Plants — Yellow Firecracker Fern
Toptropicals — Russelia equisetiformis

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants after all frost danger has passed, in fertile, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this Dunstan family selection from Alstonville, Australia grows into a large shrub or small tree where winters stay frost-free.

directions: Alstonville is a widely grown princess flower selection valued for its dense, velvety dark green foliage and heavy production of large, rich purple, five-petaled flowers from late summer into winter, later and longer than many other tibouchinas. Left unpruned in frost-free areas it develops into a substantial large shrub or small tree, but it also responds well to hard pruning each spring to keep it as a mid-size border or container specimen in zone 9. Plant in fertile, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, and protect from frost, which will cause significant dieback.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society / Wikipedia — Tibouchina lepidota
Plantmark Wholesale Nursery (Australia) — Tibouchina lepidota 'Alstonville'

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants or rooted cuttings after all frost danger has passed, in fertile, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in partial shade; this hybrid between C. thomsoniae and C. splendens needs a trellis or support to scramble over.

directions: Clerodendrum x speciosum is a hybrid between the familiar bleeding heart vine (C. thomsoniae) and the scarlet glorybower (C. splendens), combining traits of both parents into dense, terminal clusters of tubular red flowers set against a persistent, pale calyx tinged pink to white. The scrambling, semi-woody vine blooms through the warm months in spring and summer and benefits from a trellis, arbor, or fence to climb, or can be allowed to sprawl through a shrub border. Grow it in fertile, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial shade, since full tropical sun can scorch the foliage in the Gulf Coast summer. Where winters dip below freezing it dies back but often resprouts from the roots if heavily mulched.
sources: Taylor & Francis — Clerodendrum speciosum (ornamental horticulture reference)
Shrubz.us — Red Bleeding Heart Vine, Clerodendrum x speciosum

common_name: Starcluster Appleblossom Pentas (Soft Pink-and-White Egyptian Star Cluster)

planting.note: Set out transplants after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; this heat-tolerant bedding series stays compact and uniform, well suited to mass plantings and containers.

directions: Starcluster Appleblossom bears soft pink flowers that fade toward a paler, nearly white throat, giving each cluster a gentle, two-toned blush distinct from the more saturated solid colors of other pentas bedding series. Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and water regularly during establishment; once rooted in, it tolerates Gulf Coast heat and humidity with ease and draws butterflies and hummingbirds throughout the summer. The compact, uniform habit of this series makes it reliable for mass color in beds and borders as well as patio containers. In zone 9b and warmer, established plants may survive a mild winter and resprout from the base.
sources: Gardencentermarketing.com plant database — Pentas lanceolata Starcluster series
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Pentas lanceolata

common_name: Falling Star Rose Pentas (Trailing Egyptian Star Cluster)

planting.note: Set out transplants after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; unlike upright bedding pentas, this trailing selection is bred for hanging baskets and mixed container rims.

directions: Falling Star Rose is a trailing pentas selection, a departure from the upright, mounding habit of most bedding pentas series, with cascading stems carrying clusters of warm rose-pink, star-shaped flowers that spill attractively over the rim of a hanging basket or mixed container. Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and water regularly, since its shallow basket-grown roots dry out faster than in-ground plantings. It draws butterflies and hummingbirds all summer and continues blooming until frost. Treat as an annual in zone 9 unless overwintered indoors in a bright, frost-free location.
sources: Gardencentermarketing.com plant database — Pentas lanceolata Falling Star series
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Pentas lanceolata

common_name: Bahama Lavender Pentas (Compact Lavender Egyptian Star Cluster)

planting.note: Set out transplants after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; a compact bedding selection suited to borders, mass plantings, and containers.

directions: Bahama Lavender produces clusters of soft lavender, star-shaped flowers on a compact, well-branched plant that holds its shape without staking through the heat of a Gulf Coast summer. Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and water regularly during establishment; once rooted in it tolerates heat and humidity with ease and flowers continuously from late spring until frost, attracting butterflies and hummingbirds. Its small, uniform habit makes it a reliable choice for edging beds, mass color plantings, and mixed containers. In zone 9b and warmer, established plants occasionally survive a mild winter and resprout from the base.
sources: Gardencentermarketing.com plant database — Pentas lanceolata 'Bahama Lavender'
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Pentas lanceolata

common_name: Mayan Compact Purple Ruellia (Fruitless Dwarf Mexican Petunia)

planting.note: Set out divisions or nursery transplants once soil has warmed after the last frost, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; a University of Florida-bred fruitless selection developed to reduce the seed-spread invasiveness of older Mexican petunia cultivars.

directions: Mayan Compact Purple is a fruitless Mexican petunia cultivar bred at the University of Florida specifically to curb the reseeding that made older Ruellia simplex selections invasive in natural areas, while keeping a shorter, more branched, and more compact habit than the earlier 'Mayan Purple' release. It bears the same funnel-shaped, deep purple flowers over narrow, dark green foliage from late spring through fall. Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; it tolerates heat, humidity, and periodic drought once established and spreads modestly by rhizome rather than by seed. Divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor and shape.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Assessment — Ruellia simplex 'Mayan Compact Purple'
Proceedings of the Florida State Horticultural Society — Fruitless Ruellia simplex R12-2-1 ('Mayan Compact Purple')
